newsitem.title: ITALY: Russia basically not a grain importer - Zaveryukha.
newsitem.headline: Russia basically not a grain importer - Zaveryukha.

text.p: Russia's top agriculture official reiterated on Thursday that Russia can nowadays survive without significant grain imports but acknowledged that meat and dairy imports created problems for some farmers.
"We should note that Russia is basically not an importer of grains, potatoes, vegetables and other staple foods," deputy prime minister Alexander Zaveryukha told a U.N. food summit.
He made no reference to Russia's immediate grain situation.
Western grain trade sources have said in recent weeks that some Russian banks and other organisations may be trying to put together import deals but no big contracts have emerged.

Moscow agriculture sources in late October shrugged off market talk that Russia was soon planning to import large quantities of North American or Australian wheat for its far east, but did not rule out small buys over a period.

Zaveryukha, responsible for agriculture under prime minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, told leaders at the World Food Summit that Russia was pushing forward agricultural reforms but already had one of the most open regimes towards external trade.

"However, the overall unfavourable economic situation and the serious financial difficulties could not but affect the situation in agriculture," creating price disparities between the world market and prices paid to Russian farmers, he said.

"While meat and dairy products are imported, agricultural producers in Russia are experiencing difficulties in selling their products, particularly meat products," an official summit translation said.

Farm analysts say economic problems have forced cattle breeders to slash their herd numbers in recent years, helping Russia to reduce its grain imports to a fraction of their level when a previous world food conference was held in 1974.
Most observers expect private Russian importers to buy up to 1.5 million tonnes of Western wheat and flour in the current crop year, but direct government involvement is unlikely.
